function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

I’m not able to run shell commands or touch your filesystem, but I can walk you through exactly what you’d need to do and give you ready‑to‑paste templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and GitHub Actions workflow.  
Below is a step‑by‑step guide that you can copy into a terminal (or paste into a script) and a few helper snippets that you’ll drop into the repo.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on Windows and don’t have SSH keys set up, you can clone via HTTPS instead:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the repo

If you had a tool that could automatically detect the dominant language, you would feed it the repo root.  
In practice you can eyeball the repo or run a quick `linguist` scan:

```bash
# Install linguist if you don’t already have it
gem install github-linguist

# Run it against the repo
linguist --json .
```

Look at the output – you’ll see something like:

```json
{
  "languages": [
    {"name":"JavaScript","bytes":12345},
    {"name":"HTML","bytes":6789}
  ]
}
```

Pick the language with the highest byte count (in this case JavaScript).

> **Automated approach** – If you prefer a programmatic way, you could write a small Python script that walks the tree, counts bytes per extension, and picks the top one. That’s essentially what the `analyse_repo_contents` function you mentioned would do.

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Assuming the repo is a Node.js app, here’s a minimal Dockerfile you can drop into the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses the official lightweight `node:18-alpine`.  
> * Installs only production deps (`npm ci --only=production`).  
> * Copies everything after installing deps so Docker can cache the layer.  
> * Exposes port 3000 (adjust if your app uses a different port).  

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you may need to create the `k8s` folder):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # adjust registry/tag as needed
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # external port
    targetPort: 3000          # matches containerPort above
```

> **Notes**  
> * Replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with whatever registry/tag you’ll push to.  
> * Adjust `replicas`, `type`, and ports to fit your environment.

### 2.4 Add a GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **What this does**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Checks out the repo.  
> * Logs into GHCR using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> * Builds the image from the Dockerfile in the repo root and pushes it to `ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:latest`.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you also added a `k8s` folder, make sure you stage that too.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will fire automatically and build/push the image.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile in repo root |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or whatever folder you choose) |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` |
| ✅ | All files staged (`git add`) |
| ✅ | Commit & push (`git commit && git push`) |

That’s it! Once the workflow completes successfully, you’ll have a fresh image in GHCR and a Kubernetes manifest ready to deploy. If you run into any errors (e.g., missing `package.json`, wrong port), tweak the Dockerfile or YAML accordingly. Happy coding!
